extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations (PR managers, communicators, PR students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and programming public relations programs: using research to define problems, set goals and objectives, identify target publics, and choose strategies and tactics that align with organizational mission. Emphasizes working theory, tailored publics, and methods for defining and segmenting audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research as the foundational step
rubrics_metrics.description: Research initiates, monitors, and concludes the problem-solving process; it is the essential ingredient that makes public relations a management function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research is necessary not only to evaluate program impact but also to define the problem situation. Without research, practitioners cannot plan strategy, monitor progress, or evaluate success. The chapter emphasizes that planning and program decisions must be built on research-derived understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of benchmark (baseline) data
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmark data serve as the basis for monitoring the program in progress and for evaluating program effectiveness at the end of each program cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must collect baseline measures during problem-definition so later monitoring and evaluation can compare program outcomes against where they started. The chapter references a 'benchmarks model' and ties benchmark use to all three program phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of methods across phases
rubrics_metrics.description: The methods and measures used in the evaluation phase must be the same as those used in the problem-definition phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you change measurement methods between baseline and evaluation, you cannot validly determine program success or failure. Use the same instruments and definitions for comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals must reflect research-defined problems/opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations goals should reflect the problems or opportunities defined in the research step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals are derived from situation analysis; they should address the specific issues revealed by research rather than abstract or generic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals must align with organizational mission and operational goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations goals should never stand in isolation; they must make sense within the context of the organization’s broader vision, its mission, and its operational goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vision, mission, values, and managerial commitment provide the framework for PR goals and objectives. Statements of organizational goals and values help commit the organization to accountability and guide program planning, budgeting, staffing, and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close linkage among goal, objectives, strategies, and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a close linkage between the overall program goal, the objectives established for each of the publics, and the strategies and tactics selected to accomplish each objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planning requires that objectives be directly connected to the goal and that chosen strategies/tactics are clearly intended to achieve those objectives. Plans should be tailored; avoid activities that count but do not contribute to outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic planning steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a public relations goal is set, the next steps are identifying key publics, articulating objectives, and determining strategies and tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although each plan is unique, this sequence—identify publics → write objectives → choose strategies/tactics—is a consistent framework for developing a final PR plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pseudoplanning; planning is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Skimping on the strategic planning step leads to programs that may reinforce controversy, waste resources on irrelevant audiences, or facilitate misunderstanding instead of clarification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common excuses ('We don’t have time', 'Things change too fast', 'We get paid for results not planning', 'We're doing okay without a plan') are rebutted: planning saves time overall, plans are adaptable, clients pay for results achieved according to a plan, and short-term successes can fail without contingency planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working theory drives strategy and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: The program strategy usually represents someone’s working theory of what has to be done to achieve a desired outcome; it is 'an idea of how things might work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working theory should guide every program decision (e.g., why a tactic is chosen). It must be more than gut feeling: practitioners should ground working theories in established communication and PR theories backed by research and experience and continually devise and test them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target publics must be specifically defined (avoid 'general public')
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective programs communicate and build relationships with specifically defined 'target publics' or 'strategic publics.' The concept of a general or mass public holds little value in PR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should discard vague notions of 'the general public' and instead select, define, segment, and target publics with sufficient detail to measure opinion, set objectives, craft messages, select media, and evaluate outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reification of publics and practical limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Target publics are frequently abstractions imposed by program planners; reification (treating an abstraction as concrete) is necessary to develop objectives, strategies, and tactics, though it involves approximations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given limited resources, practitioners often must treat groups as concrete segments. Reification is practical but requires careful, informed definition—targeting individuals is ideal but usually impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-situational (demographic/psychographic) segmentation is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-situational publics are groups identifiable by something they have in common (age, gender, lifestyle) regardless of situation; such approaches provide minimal guidance for strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demographics and geographics are useful for selecting media and allocating resources but are insufficient alone for developing strategy; they should be combined with situation-based information about involvement and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situational definitions of publics (Grunig’s situational theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Situational theory predicts whether publics will be latent, aware, or active in a specific situation using three factors: problem recognition, level of involvement, and constraint recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situational definitions focus on how people are involved or affected by the specific problem situation and are more useful for strategy than cross-situational traits. The theory helps identify which publics will seek information (active) versus merely process information (passive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three predictive factors: problem recognition, level of involvement, constraint recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem recognition: extent people are aware something is missing or amiss; Level of involvement: extent people see themselves affected by the situation; Constraint recognition: extent people feel limited by external factors versus able to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These variables predict communicative behavior: higher problem recognition and involvement and lower perceived constraints increase the likelihood of information seeking and active communication/organizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information behavior distinctions: information seeking vs information processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Active communication behavior is information seeking (planned scanning); passive behavior is information processing (may or may not attend to messages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distinctions when tailoring messages: publics likely to seek information require different message forms and channels than passive publics who primarily process incidental messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of publics (problem-solving orientations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies produce four types of publics: (1) All-issue publics—active on all issues; (2) Apathetic publics—inattentive and inactive; (3) Single-issue publics—active on one or a limited number of related issues; (4) Hot-issue publics—active after media coverage exposes almost everyone to the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying which type a public falls into informs the intensity, timing, and channels of outreach and the kinds of objectives and strategies appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor messages to publics based on activity and issue importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Messages must be individually tailored to fit the information needs of different publics, based on how active or passive their communication behavior is and what issues are important to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Message design should account for publics' likelihood to seek, attend to, select, and transmit information (STOPS framework). One-size-fits-all messaging is ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to include when defining publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Useful definitions of program publics include how people are involved in or affected by the problem situation, who they are, where they live, what relevant organizations they belong to, and what they do that is relevant to the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions should derive from the particular situation for which the intervention is planned, not merely from shared cross-situational traits; these details help set objectives, choose media, and measure outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to defining publics (geographics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographics—natural or political boundaries—indicate where to find people but give little useful insight about important differences within the boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographic segmentation is useful for selecting media outlets and allocating program resources according to population density (ZIP codes, area codes, city/county lines), but not sufficient for strategic message design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to defining publics (demographics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demographics—gender, income, age, marital status, education—are the most frequently used individual characteristics but provide little understanding of why or how people are involved or affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demographics help make an initial cut but must be supplemented with situation-specific information to guide strategy and tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to defining publics (psychographics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychographics—psychological and lifestyle characteristics—segment people by values and personality traits (e.g., VALS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychographics can be useful but typically only when combined with attributes that tie segments to a particular situation (i.e., when linked to involvement or issue relevance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to defining publics (covert power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Covert power—behind-the-scenes political or economic power—describes people at the top of a power pyramid who operate across situations and exert influence in ways not always easily observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying covert power requires observation over time, interviews with insiders, document analysis, or combinations thereof; these actors can be critical to strategy despite low visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to defining publics (position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Position uses the positions held by individuals (roles) rather than their personal attributes to identify target publics important because of their roles in a particular situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify people whose formal roles make them influential in achieving program goals (e.g., officials, managers, board members) and tailor objectives and tactics to their positional influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to defining publics (reputation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation (listed as an approach) identifies publics by their standing or perceived influence in a community or issue set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation-based targeting focuses on actors known to shape opinion or behavior; use reputation alongside other approaches to refine target lists.
